---
title: "AI Tools and Lab Data"
description: "Which data can go into which AI tools, and what you're responsible for when you use them."
---

AI assistants and coding agents are useful in the lab, for writing and debugging
code and for drafting text. They also send what they read to someone else's
servers. This page sets out which data can go into which tools. If you're not
sure which category something falls into, treat it as the most restricted one
and ask Tomás.

## Tools

- **The lab's Claude organization:** Claude and Claude Code through the lab's
  Team plan. Anthropic doesn't use conversations, files, or data from it to
  train its models. Use this for lab work; ask Tomás for a seat.
- **Local models:** models that run on your own computer or a lab server (for
  example with Ollama). Nothing leaves the machine.
- **Personal accounts:** your own ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or similar.
  What you enter may be used to train models, and it isn't covered by any lab
  agreement.

If you also have a personal Claude account, check which one you're using: in
Claude Code, `/status` shows your organization, which should be Omnia Lab.

## What can go where

| Data | Lab Claude organization | Local model | Personal account |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public data, published papers, code in public repos | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Lab code in private repos, unpublished results, manuscript and grant drafts | Yes | Yes | No |
| Controlled-access data, obtained under a data use agreement | No | Only on systems the agreement allows | No |
| Participant or patient data | No | Only where the project's ethics approval allows | No |
| Others' confidential work, such as manuscripts or grants you're reviewing | If the journal or funder allows it | If the journal or funder allows it | No |

Data use agreements usually forbid sharing data with third parties, and an AI
service is a third party, even through the lab's account and even though it
doesn't train on your data.

## Coding agents read your files

Coding agents like Claude Code don't only see what you paste into them. They
read files in the folder you start them in, and the output of the commands they
run (`head data.csv`, `print(df)`) goes to the model too. So:

- **Work with agents on code, not on restricted data.** Develop against public
  or synthetic data, like the small synthetic dataset in the
  [scRNA-seq spec lab](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC/ibm3407-scrna-spec-lab),
  then run the finished code on the real data yourself.
- **Keep restricted data outside any folder you open an agent in.** This also
  keeps it out of Git.
- **Read commands before you approve them**, especially ones that open or print
  data files.

## Your responsibilities

- **You own the result.** Check AI-written code and text as carefully as your
  own: read it, run it, test it. "The AI wrote it" doesn't explain a mistake.
- **Understand what you submit.** If you can't explain a piece of code in your
  pull request, ask about it before submitting.
- **Disclose AI use** where a journal, funder, or course requires it, and tell
  your co-authors.
- **Keep secrets out of prompts:** no passwords, API keys, or tokens.

If you think restricted data went into an AI tool, tell Tomás right away.
